=== DIN_Project_58482_Final.docx ===
September 4, 2026
Public Utility Commission of Texas
1701 N. Congress Avenue
P.O. Box 13326
Austin, Texas 78711-3326
RE:  Project No. 58482, Large Load Demand Management Service; Comments of the Digital Infrastructure Network on Proposed New 16 TAC Section 25.521
Dear Commissioners:
The Digital Infrastructure Network ("DIN") respectfully submits these comments on proposed new 16 TAC Section 25.521, relating to the Large Load Demand Management Service (LLDMS). DIN appreciates the Commission seeking input from the large-load customers the service is intended to engage. DIN represents companies across data centers, advanced computing, energy, digital assets, quantum, and related infrastructure. DIN members include large-load operators that are interested in participating in LLDMS and helping ERCOT develop a workable, voluntary reliability service. [1]
DIN supports LLDMS as a voluntary, competitively procured, performance-based service. A program created to procure demand reductions from large loads will succeed only if customers capable of offering measurable and nonduplicative megawatts have a clear path to qualify, offer, perform, and be compensated. The final rule should focus on the aggregate electrical result at the qualifying site and should not prescribe tenant-, rack-, or equipment-specific methods that may not be within the large-load customer's contractual or operational control. [1][2]
ERCOT's experience with demand response shows that flexible demand can support reliability when reductions are defined, measurable, and dependable. LLDMS can build on that principle by allowing qualified large loads to make a voluntary commitment in advance and compete to provide the reduction ERCOT procures. [3]
I.  LLDMS Should Provide a Practical Path for Qualified Large Loads to Participate
PURA Section 39.170 establishes both coordinated firm-load-shed readiness for certain transmission-voltage customers and a separate voluntary service through which ERCOT competitively procures demand reduction. The final rule should preserve that distinction. Firm-load-shed readiness should neither automatically enroll a customer in LLDMS nor prevent a qualified customer from electing to participate. [2]
DIN members are interested in participating, but the amount and form of available reduction will vary by site design, commercial arrangements, and operating conditions. A customer should be permitted to offer the aggregate site-level reduction it can reasonably commit and verify. Before qualification or bidding, ERCOT should publish the commercial and technical terms needed to understand the obligation, including the measurement point, baseline, notice, duration, QSE responsibilities, settlement, and performance requirements.
Application opportunities should be predictable and frequent and ERCOT should identify deficiencies in writing, provide applicants adequate time to submit information and cure deficiencies, and use the ordinary ERCOT appeal process for denials or suspensions. The Commission should not impose a rigid decision shot clock, any implementation deadlines should leave applicants sufficient time to complete the required showing.
II.  Eligibility and Performance Should Be Determined at the Qualifying Site
The proposed rule defines a large load customer by total non-coincident peak demand at a single site. An LLDMS offer, deployment, and settlement should therefore be evaluated at the qualifying site or applicable grid interface, not at the level of an individual tenant, rack, or workload. Where ERCOT treats a campus with multiple buildings or facilities as one qualifying site, the customer and its QSE should be able to aggregate reductions across that site into one offer. ERCOT should then pay the applicable market-based compensation for the verified aggregate megawatts delivered under that award, without requiring separate tenant- or building-level offers or payments. [1]
DIN supports clear enforcement of PURA's restrictions on participation in other listed programs and services. Rather than presume that a customer can divide capability among tenants, equipment, or internal functions, ERCOT should publish a prospective eligibility chart explaining how each listed program or arrangement affects a qualifying site. That guidance should be available before enrollment and should identify the circumstances that create prohibited duplicate procurement or compensation. A customer should not be excluded based on an after-the-fact or undisclosed interpretation of overlapping participation.
ERCOT's current Batch Zero framework recognizes Withdrawal-Limited Private Use Network and Bring Your Own Generation configurations as part of the large-load interconnection landscape. LLDMS implementation should be consistent with that market direction. WLPUN/BYOG arrangements, battery storage, lawful on-site generation, and facility-level controls should not be disqualifying on their face. Depending on a site's actual design and operating arrangements, those tools may support an aggregate reduction in grid withdrawal, and should such be encouraged. Eligibility should be on whether the qualifying site can offer a measurable reduction under ERCOT-approved requirements without prohibited duplicate commitment or compensation. [4]
III.  Procurement, Compensation, and Accountability Should Encourage Participation
DIN supports as-needed, risk-based procurement through competitive offers. Before offers are due, each request for proposals and resulting agreement should state the obligation period, applicable location, awarded megawatts, measurement and baseline approach, notice, expected duration, settlement method, and material performance consequences. The statutory 24-hour notice should be preserved so participants can determine whether they can safely and lawfully meet the requested site-level reduction. [1][2]
DIN supports allowing eligible sites to provide locationally effective relief during a defined transmission emergency when the reduction can address a material risk of firm load shed. That authority should not become routine congestion management or substitute for necessary transmission investment.
Compensation should be awarded when the obligation is satisfied. A qualifying site that performs should receive the applicable market-clearing payment for the verified aggregate megawatts delivered under its award, regardless of how the customer lawfully allocates the reduction within the site. Verified capacity that was reserved and available but not deployed should receive an availability payment at an amount the Commission determines is appropriate to reflect the obligation undertaken and support competitive participation. DIN does not recommend a fixed percentage in these comments and takes no position on the proposed annual program budget.
Settlement and enforcement should be proportionate to actual performance. ERCOT should publish the material standards in advance, distinguish customer performance from QSE, metering, utility, or system issues, provide notice and the ordinary appeal process, and allow a corrected deficiency to support reinstatement. These protections promote accountability without turning a limited deficiency into exclusion from the program.
As ERCOT develops the protocols and other implementation details necessary for LLDMS, DIN encourages a transparent stakeholder process that includes prospective large-load participants and their QSEs. Material qualification, measurement, deployment, settlement, and performance requirements should be established prospectively so interested customers can evaluate participation. Any public after-action reporting should provide sufficient information to evaluate program performance while protecting customer-specific operating, tenant, and security-sensitive information.
IV.  Conclusion
DIN supports adoption of LLDMS as a voluntary, competitive reliability service and appreciates the Commission inviting large-load input. DIN members are interested in participating. The final rule should provide measure eligibility and performance at the qualifying site, clearly identify the effect of participation in other programs, recognize current large-load configurations on a technology-neutral basis, disclose the material obligation before bidding, compensate aggregate availability and performance, and apply appropriate accountability.
With those principles, LLDMS can add dependable demand-side capability to ERCOT while allowing prospective participants to determine what site-level reduction they can safely and reliably offer. DIN looks forward to working with the Commission, ERCOT, QSEs, utilities, consumer representatives, and other stakeholders as the implementing protocols are developed.
Respectfully submitted,
DIGITAL INFRASTRUCTURE NETWORK
______________________________
Spencer Ward
Policy & Technology Director
Digital Infrastructure Network
spencer@digitalinfranetl.org
References. [1] PUCT, Project No. 58482, Proposal for Publication of New 16 TAC Section 25.521, 51 Tex. Reg. 5323-5325 (Aug. 14, 2026). [2] PURA Section 39.170, enacted by S.B. 6, 89th Leg., R.S. (2025). [3] ERCOT, Demand Response; Emergency Response Service; Load Resource Participation in the ERCOT Markets. [4] ERCOT, PGRR145/NPRR1325, Batch Zero Process for Large Load Interconnections; Market Notice M-B062326-02, Batch Zero Follow-Up for WLPUN/BYOG (June 26, 2026).
